title: Looking for tools which help me make games rather than just vibe coding it or ai generate it
author: Useful-Course-9620
selftext: Hi, I am new to gamedev. I know a little bit of programming and I have never touched the blender or anything art related. I wanted to use ai, so it can help me with making assets and code easily rather than generating itself. I am not aiming for high quality or high poly assets so all I need is something that can reduce the friction between my instructions and software. I know mcp servers and cli exist. But i don't want something that will drain out tokens just to add a cube. And tools which can help me build and correct animation etc. rather than just generating it. So i wanted to know if there are tools which are more like multimodal auto correct/completion than generator. I know the corrector and completion do generation. But I hope you get the idea.

comments.author: Hot-Middle7260
comments.body: just ask codex/claudecode to teach you the basics. Have a conversation with it  its literally your own personal tutor 24/7 and lives inside your computer and have access to infinite amount of resources and can even use your game dev engines natively too.

replies.author: DealerIcy3439
replies.body: I just for Claude and he is 100 a useful fella, asks lot of questions and can help construct a guide and plan

replies.author: wakeofchaos
replies.body: Yeah I feel like this is probably the most underrated thing about ai assistance

comments.author: couldgiveaflyingfck
comments.body:
No one is hand-coding anymore. Sounds like social media might be influencing your perspective.

I have four friends who are senior software engineers with 15–20+ years of hands-on coding experience. One owns a business, one works at GoDaddy, and the other two work at a $2 billion company. All four have stopped hand-coding within the past five months or less.

At their companies, junior software engineers have been let go en masse, and everyone now gets a weekly token budget to work with AI. The industry is changing rapidly, and what was standard practice just a few months ago is already becoming a thing of the past.

replies.author: Embarrassed_Split236
replies.body: That’s assuming you know what to ask AI though, idk if you can really set up what you want by just letting the AI roll the dice with its interpretation of the code you’d want. I’d expect someone going straight to AI without the preliminary knowledge would be way more inefficient at troubleshooting too, which goes back to the issue of burning tokens. Maybe you can just ask it to break down everything it writes and learn that way though.

replies.author: Useful-Course-9620
replies.body: I understand that. I am not asking for hand-coding. But I don't want to just prompt once, get an over complicated or complex answer/model in 1 min. Then checking  it why it it feels wrong and describe what to have what not for 30 min and pay it gets it right. I just don't want to teleport to a finish line and then run back and teleport again. I want to start from scratch and then built one thing at a time. So I can control what is being added and what not. So I have easier time maintaining it.

replies.author: fapfap_ahh
replies.body: General AI skills (superpowers repo for example) will help you here to be honest. There are also articles and guides on how to be an "AI director" rather a prompter which is where you want to be.

comments.author: Hot_Professional8287
comments.body:
I think what you're looking for is going to be the best thing ever when it happens, and it's what a lot of us are attempting to build right now - a framework for *multi-modal* harmony between artist and agent. Those frameworks are being built all over the world by a lot of people, but until they're released, your best bet is to use AI to learn faster, and connect tools like Blender to your agents via MCP, so they can guide you.

As you get more skilled, you'll start whipping together your own tools that strike the right balance between authorship and automation.

replies.body: I’m finding this to be pretty helpful myself. Ask it what tools can help build out your game more. It made me a map maker tool for building dungeon layouts that is pretty interesting.

replies.body: I lost count of the amount of customsoftware for developing i produced.  tools, plugins, scripts and even some full fledget apps. Its a blessing

comments.author: 328amdev
comments.body: AI-assisted suggestion: use the model to help build a small reusable editor tool, rather than asking it to perform the same operation each time. For your low-poly workflow, examples could be a button to batch-rename parts, set pivots, or check export settings. Once written and checked, the tool runs locally without another model call. Start with one operation on a throwaway asset and verify the result before applying it to the rest. For animation feedback, an annotated screenshot plus one specific question is a narrower task than asking an agent to fix the whole rig. Which part is causing the most friction right now: modeling, rigging, animation, or getting assets into the engine?

comments.author: OddBallGameDev
comments.body: Pick a game engine, find a course on YouTube, and start learning. No tool is going to save you from inexperience. Learning how to make good games takes a long, long time and lots of bad games in the process. That hasn't changed with AI. Start with the part you are most interested in and make connections or find assets for the rest

comments.author: Excellent_Space_2178
comments.body:
Heyoo! I think you're on the right track by wanting to control the process rather than just plugging in a prompt and praying it works. That approach will get you much further in the long run.

I'd recommend what others have mentioned here: a) experimenting with vibe coding tools and b) **START LEARNING!**

There are some great resources out there. One I've recently picked up myself is [boot.dev](https://boot.dev), where I'm learning to code.

I actually wrote a little about this exact topic on my Substack [**On GenAI Use in Creative Media — My experiments with AI and game development**](https://substack.com/@kostisspyroglou)

**One thing that surprised me was how much work can still go into fixing an AI-generated asset.** Sometimes you end up spending more time cleaning up the result than you would have spent making it yourself. It made me question whether AI is actually removing friction or just moving it somewhere else.

comments.author: derLeisemitderLaute
comments.body: I would suggest you do a little test game for the things you want to add. Then you let Claude implement it and explain the code. There you can ask it about everything. After you done that you make your own game piece by piece with what you learned from Claude.

comments.author: DamnageBeats
comments.body: I am working on a tool that helps make a template with all the logic built in so all you have to do is drop assets where you want them and the logic they need is already made. If it’s an npc it knows to give it npc routines, if they are props for the stage like trees or whatever, they get their collision. I’ve been working on it for quite some time, developing the different parts of the system, different genres etc.
